name: Council of Chalcedon
summary: The council that defined Christ as one person in two natures, divine and human, using Pope Leo I's Tome, and that split the eastern churches.
place: Chalcedon, across the Bosporus from Constantinople (modern Kadıköy, Istanbul)

end.label: Council closes after defining Christ as one person in two natures

background.text: In 449 a council at Ephesus under Dioscorus of Alexandria restored the monk Eutyches, who taught that Christ had only one nature after the incarnation, and deposed Flavian of Constantinople, who died soon after from mistreatment. Leo I called it a 'robber council' (latrocinium).
After Emperor Theodosius II died in 450, the new emperor Marcian and Empress Pulcheria summoned a new council to reverse Ephesus 449.

happened.text: Around 350–500 bishops met, nearly all from the East; imperial officials presided over the sessions and controlled the agenda, with Leo's legates given the first place among the bishops.
The bishops read and accepted Leo's Tome to Flavian; the minutes record the acclamation 'Peter has spoken through Leo'.
On 22 October the council issued its definition: Christ is one person 'acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation'.
It deposed Dioscorus of Alexandria and restored bishops removed in 449, including Theodoret of Cyrrhus and Ibas of Edessa after they condemned Nestorius.
Canon 28 gave Constantinople, as 'New Rome', privileges equal to Old Rome and second rank after it; Leo's legates protested, and Leo refused to confirm the canon.

participants.name: Marcian and Pulcheria
participants.role: Emperor and empress who summoned the council; Marcian attended the sixth session

participants.name: Leo I
participants.role: Bishop of Rome; his Tome became the basis of the definition, and his legates (Paschasinus, Lucentius, Boniface) led the bishops

participants.name: Anatolius of Constantinople
participants.role: Bishop of the capital; supported canon 28

participants.name: Dioscorus of Alexandria
participants.role: Bishop who presided at Ephesus 449; deposed

participants.name: Theodoret of Cyrrhus
participants.role: Theologian deposed in 449 and restored at the council

outcomes.text: The Chalcedonian definition became the standard teaching on Christ for the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and most Protestant churches.

Much of Egypt, Syria, and Armenia rejected the council as a betrayal of Cyril of Alexandria's teaching; they formed the churches now called Oriental Orthodox (Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean), and the split has never been formally healed.

Imperial attempts to reconcile the two sides, such as Zeno's Henotikon (482) and later monothelitism, failed and caused further schisms, including the Acacian schism between Rome and Constantinople (484–519).
Rome's refusal of canon 28 marked an early stage in the rivalry between Rome and Constantinople.

condemnations.authority: Council of bishops under imperial oversight
condemnations.reason: Dioscorus of Alexandria deposed, formally for refusing to appear when summoned three times and for his conduct at Ephesus 449 rather than for heresy
condemnations.status: Rejected by the Coptic and other Oriental Orthodox churches, which venerate him as a saint

condemnations.reason: Eutyches's teaching of one nature after the union condemned, confirming his deposition of 448
condemnations.status: Not reversed; the Oriental Orthodox churches also reject Eutyches

persecution_note: The council was followed by decades of violence between supporters and opponents of its definition, with the imperial government enforcing it by force.

persecution.title: Exile of Dioscorus
persecution.summary: After his deposition Dioscorus was banished by imperial order to Gangra in Paphlagonia, where he died in 454.

responsible.name: Council of Chalcedon
responsible.jurisdiction: Church of the Eastern Roman Empire

persecution.title: Murder of Proterius of Alexandria
persecution.summary: Proterius, the pro-Chalcedon bishop installed in Alexandria with military support, faced riots from the start. After Marcian's death, an anti-Chalcedon crowd killed him in 457, and Timothy Aelurus took his see.

responsible.name: Supporters of Timothy Aelurus
responsible.role: Rival bishop who benefited; sources disagree on his personal part

persecution.outcome: Proterius killed; Emperor Leo I later exiled Timothy Aelurus (460).

sources.citation: Richard Price and Michael Gaddis (trans. and eds.), The Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, 3 vols. Translated Texts for Historians 45. Liverpool: Liverpool University Press, 2005.
Norman P. Tanner (ed.), Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils, vol. 1. London: Sheed & Ward; Washington, DC: Georgetown University Press, 1990.
Leo the Great, Letter 28 (the Tome to Flavian), 449, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 12.

decisions: Dogma: Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, 'without confusion, change, division, or separation'; Leo's Tome accepted; Dioscorus deposed.
